If a single target is needed, keep the directorate's 5 (University) / 6 (Elite) as flat targets.

card_setEff.note: No published set-efficiency norms using the (+ minus -)/attempts formula were found. Kept the approved University 30, mapped Elite 45 to international, and interpolated evenly.

card_digEff.note: No published dig-efficiency norms using this formula were found. Kept the approved University 5, mapped Elite 20 to international, and interpolated evenly.

card_blockPerSet.note: The only published figure is Olympic block success (18.6% M, 17% W); no per-player per-set norms were found. Kept the approved University 0.3, mapped Elite 0.6 to international, and interpolated. Middle blockers will sit well above these all-position values.

card_battingSR.note: Elite mapped to international (the approved Elite values match IPL/T20I and men's ODI international norms); levels between are even interpolation. Women use the approved targets, which equal the men's, but women's T20I/ODI norms are well below them (T20I ~105-120); the directorate should revisit.

card_battingAvg.note: Elite mapped to international (the approved Elite values match IPL/T20I and men's ODI international norms); levels between are even interpolation.

card_batDotPct.note: Elite mapped to international (the approved Elite values match IPL/T20I and men's ODI international norms); levels between are even interpolation. The lowest IPL 2026 dot-ball % among batters was ~25-26%. No ODI target and no level-graded ODI data, so ODI is null.

sources: November et al. (2025) Determinants of success in ODI and T20 cricket: systematic review, Applied Sciences 15(19):10341 - https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/15/19/10341
card_boundaryPct.note: Elite mapped to international (the approved Elite values match IPL/T20I and men's ODI international norms); levels between are even interpolation. Winning T20 sides hit ~3.9 more fours and ~1.9 more sixes (November 2025). No ODI target or level data, so ODI is null.

card_controlPct.note: Elite mapped to international (the approved Elite values match IPL/T20I and men's ODI international norms); levels between are even interpolation. No public level-graded false-shot data found.

card_economy.note: T20 is null (rule 4): the approved Elite 8.5 is worse than University 7.5 because economy rises against stronger batting. ODI keeps the approved 5.5→5.0; it is also opposition-sensitive, so treat it with care. Elite mapped to international (the approved Elite values match IPL/T20I and men's ODI international norms); levels between are even interpolation.

card_bowlSR.note: Elite mapped to international (the approved Elite values match IPL/T20I and men's ODI international norms); levels between are even interpolation.

card_bowlAvg.note: Approved University = Elite = 25, so the ladders are flat. The T20 targets agree with each other (7.5x20/6=25, 8.5x18/6≈25.5). ODI does not: the approved economy and strike rate give 5.5x36/6=33 at university, so a flat 25 is harsh for ODI. Worth revisiting.

card_bowlDotPct.note: Null (rule 4): the approved T20 Elite 40 is worse than University 45 because dot % falls against stronger batting. No ODI target, and ODI has the same opposition effect.

card_boundaryConcPct.note: Null (rule 4): the approved T20 Elite 18 is worse than University 12 because boundaries conceded rise against stronger batting. No ODI target, and ODI has the same opposition effect.

sources: November et al. (2025) Determinants of success in ODI and T20 cricket: systematic review, Applied Sciences 15(19):10341 - https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/15/19/10341
card_extrasPerOver.note: Elite mapped to international (the approved Elite values match IPL/T20I and men's ODI international norms); levels between are even interpolation. Winning T20 sides bowl ~0.29 fewer no-balls per match (November 2025).

card_catchEff.note: CricViz IPL catching efficiency 75-81.5% (2023-26); women's T20 World Cup 63.9% (2024), 82% (2023), 89% (2020). Approved Elite 80 = international. Elite mapped to international (the approved Elite values match IPL/T20I and men's ODI international norms); levels between are even interpolation.

card_keeperConv.note: Elite mapped to international (the approved Elite values match IPL/T20I and men's ODI international norms); levels between are even interpolation. No public level-graded keeper data found.

card_runningEff.note: In-house +/- metric with no published norms. Elite mapped to international (the approved Elite values match IPL/T20I and men's ODI international norms); levels between are even interpolation.

card_fieldingEff.note: In-house +/- metric with no published norms. Elite mapped to international (the approved Elite values match IPL/T20I and men's ODI international norms); levels between are even interpolation.

sprint20m.note: No badminton 20 m sprint norms found (topendsports recommends the test with 5/10 m splits but gives no values). Estimated for electronic gates, standing start: trained court-sport men ~3.3 s rising ~2% per level; women +10%.

sources: Ooi et al. (2009) Physiological characteristics of elite and sub-elite badminton players, J Sports Sci 27(14):1591-1599
verticalJump.note: Ooi 2009: Malaysian world-ranked men CMJ 46.3 cm vs sub-elite squad 46.0 cm (no difference). App scale (30-65) matches Badminton Australia's arm-swing Sargent jump (men 'average' 41-50, 'above average' 51-60 cm), so ladder is arm-swing values ~5-10 cm above Ooi's CMJ; women ~25% lower.

handGrip.note: No adult badminton grip data in kg found. Badminton Australia NJP norms (mean of both hands): men 'average' 48-52, women 26-30 kg; Indian players (Hyderabad, mean age 15) only 26/21 kg. Estimated dominant-hand ladder; women ~65% of men. Grip discriminates level weakly.

onCourtAgility.note: The app does not fix a protocol, so values sit inside its 18-11 s scale with a ~12% spread from university to international (women ~9% slower). Ooi 2009's sideways agility test (15.3 s elite vs 15.0 s sub-elite) and four-corner test did not separate levels; Badminton Australia's on-court speed test is ~10 s.

sources: Liu et al. (2021) The Effect of Eight-Week Sprint Interval Training on Aerobic Performance of Elite Badminton Players, IJERPH 18(2):638
yoyoLevel.note: Yo-Yo IR1 levels. International: Chinese national semi-finalists ran IR2 1083 m (men) / 725 m (women), converted at an estimated IR1 ~2.1x IR2 to ~2280 m (19.6) / ~1520 m (17.3). University: Brazilian club players ran IR1 1028 m; set at 1160 m (16.2) for men. Even 280 m (men) / 200 m (women) steps between.

sources: Kavanashri et al. (2023) Anthropometry and Physical Characteristics of Indian Badminton Players, Int J Kinanthropometry
heightCm.note: National = Indian sub-elite players with national/international experience (M 175.4, W 165.2 cm). International = Chinese national semi-finalists (M ~178, W ~168), Spanish national championship (M 178, W 165), Malaysian elite (176). University estimated; zonal/state interpolated.

sources: Rojas-Valverde et al. (2020) Identification of games and sex-related activity profile in junior international badminton, Int J Perf Anal Sport
matchMetresPerMin.note: Whole-match averages including rest between rallies. U18 international juniors, UWB tracking: 44.6 (M) / 43.5 (W) m/min, mapped to national. Elite African men (10 Hz GPS): 1763 m in 35.3 min = 50 m/min, mapped to international ~48. Lower levels estimated from shorter rallies and lower work density.

matchTopSpeedKmh.note: The app reports the 95th percentile of smoothed speed, not the absolute peak. Published: max speed ~10.8-11.0 km/h (M) and ~10.4-11.0 (W) in U18 internationals; top-30 world singles footwork 2.2-2.6 m/s (8-9.4 km/h). High-school players were often as fast, so the ladder is deliberately shallow.

matchHsrPerMin.note: Null: the app's court threshold (14.4 km/h) is above the ~11 km/h maximum badminton players reach on court, so the value is ~0 at every level and cannot rank players. A badminton-specific threshold (~9 km/h) would be needed first.

matchSprintMetresPerMin.note: Null: the 18 km/h sprint threshold is never reached on a badminton court (published max ~11 km/h), so the value is 0 at every level.

matchAccelPerMin.note: Method-dependent. IMU counts are high (Guo 2025: 55.9 efforts >3 m/s2 per set; Fu 2021: ~1.7 M / 2.9 W accelerations per min). Position tracking like the app's video is closer to UWB, where the whole-match maximum averaged only 3.87 (M) / 3.47 (W) m/s2, so bursts above 3 m/s2 are rare. Estimated low; calibrate on real clips.

sources: Laffaye, Phomsoupha & Dor (2015) Changes in the game characteristics of a badminton match, J Sports Sci Med
card_wue.note: Elite mapped to international. Olympic men's singles finals: 36% winners, 23% forced errors, 41% unforced errors, a pooled W:UE of ~0.88, below both approved targets. The approved targets read as a winning player's ratio, not a level average; kept per rule 5.

card_serveWonPct.note: No published rally-won-on-serve % found (Gomez 2019 splits point outcome by serving/receiving but not win share). Between evenly matched players this sits near the structural serve (dis)advantage at every level, so it discriminates weakly. Approved targets kept; Elite = international.

card_serveErrPct.note: No published serve-fault rates found. Approved University 3 / Elite 1 kept, Elite mapped to international (serve faults are rare in elite play), with even interpolation between.

sources: Hayashi et al. (2026) Novel Analysis of Game Performance in Badminton: BWF Top-Ranking vs Regional University League Players, Applied Sciences 16(8):3819
card_receiveErrPct.note: Men's singles receive errors: BWF top-ranking 6.8% vs university league 13.6%. Approved University 12 kept (rule 5); Elite 7 matches BWF, so Elite = international. Evenly interpolated; women assumed equal (no data).

card_smashWinPct.note: Null (rule 4): smash ace rate falls as opposition defence improves. University players 15.4% after a lift and 22.3% after a clear, vs BWF 12.2% and 14.2%; after a long receive both ~24.5%. Approved 12/13 fit BWF players but would rate university players as international.

card_smashErrPct.note: Smash error rates: BWF 7.1-9.4% vs university 8.0-15.8% depending on preceding shot. Approved University 10 kept; Elite 7 matches BWF, so Elite = international; even interpolation. Women assumed equal.

card_netErrPct.note: Hayashi 2026 reports significantly lower hairpin (net) error rates and >90% rally-continuing hairpin shots for BWF players vs university players, but the exact rates were not accessible. Approved targets kept, Elite = international, even interpolation.

card_netKillPct.note: No published net-kill conversion data found. Approved targets kept, Elite = international. Like smash winners, this may fall against stronger defence; revisit with the app's own data.

card_liftNegPct.note: No published data on graded (+/-) lifts and clears. Approved University 25 / Elite 15 kept, Elite = international, even interpolation.

card_effDefence.note: Coach-graded (+ minus -) / attempts; no published equivalent found. Approved targets kept, Elite = international, even interpolation.

card_effDrop.note: Coach-graded. Hayashi 2026 found >90% rally-continuing drops and significantly fewer drop errors for BWF players, but its ace-minus-error 'effectiveness' is opposition-sensitive, and the paper's grading differs from this card's +/-. Approved targets kept, Elite = international.

sources: Axman et al. (2025) Physical Performance Tests in 8008 Competitive Youth Tennis Players - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Normative Values, European Journal of Sport Science
sprint20m.note: Meta-analysis pooled U18 competitive tennis players: boys 3.09 s, girls 3.38 s, mapped to national. The other levels are spread evenly (about 0.07-0.08 s per level), and international is estimated. The women's gap (~9-10%) matches the published sex difference.

verticalJump.note: Assumes a free-arm vertical jump, as the app's 30-65 cm anchors imply. Meta-analysis hands-on-hips CMJ for U18 players is 38 cm (boys) and 31 cm (girls); adding ~12-15% for arm swing gives about 43/35. Chinese national/international juniors aged ~15 jumped 50.6/39.6 cm. National-to-international is estimated from these. Take ~6 cm off every value if the app measures hands-on-hips CMJ.

handGrip.note: Dominant hand. Meta-analysis pooled values: U18 boys 49.9 kg (U17 49.1), U18 girls 35.8 kg (U17 37.7). Chinese elite juniors: 47.7 / 37.0 kg. Junior values were mapped to state-national, and adult international (~56/38) plus the lower levels are estimated.

onCourtAgility.note: Assumes the tennis Spider run (5 sprints from the centre of the baseline), which is the standard on-court agility test in tennis. Published values: collegiate women (ITN 5+) 18.2 s, mapped to university/zonal; elite Hungarian U18 juniors 18.05 s (boys) and 19.28 s (girls); Chinese national juniors 18.3/19.1 s. Protocols differ by ~1 s, so the adult men's and international values are estimated. Note: the app's 11-18 s anchors do not fit a Spider run.

yoyoLevel.note: Yo-Yo IR1 in speed-level.shuttle notation (M 1200-1920 m, W 840-1440 m). The only tennis data found: Chinese national/international juniors aged ~15 ran 1504 m (~17.2) and 1100 m (~16.0), mapped to state. The rest is estimated, and tennis sits well below football norms.

heightCm.note: Tour top-100 averages are ATP 188 cm (top-10 191.9) and WTA 174 cm. Those are a ceiling, not Indian international level. The ladder is estimated from Indian university population heights, stepping up about 2-3 cm per level. No Indian tennis height data was found.

matchMetresPerMin.note: Tennis GPS match play (whole match, including time between points): young players 46.0 m/min; adolescent boys 3362 m in 81 min (41 m/min). These are mapped to university-state. The footballer 105-120 m/min figure does not apply. Hawk-Eye in-point distance per point is 7.4 m (pro men) vs 6.9 m (junior boys) but 5.9 m (pro women) vs 6.3 m (junior girls), so the women's ladder is nearly flat.

matchTopSpeedKmh.note: Youth GPS peak speeds are 4.34 m/s (15.6 km/h) and 4.4 m/s (15.8 km/h). The ATP Physicality Index lists a men's-tennis maximum speed of 23.58 km/h. Adult university to international peaks are estimated between these, and women are set ~8% lower. A short filmed clip gives a lower peak than a full match.

matchHsrPerMin.note: Young players covered 0.51 m/min above 3.8 m/s (13.7 km/h), mapped to university men. The other levels are estimated. High-speed running is a tiny share of tennis movement because most movements happen within ~2.5 m.

matchSprintMetresPerMin.note: Running above 18 km/h is rare in tennis: youth peak speeds (~15.6 km/h) never reach it, and only elite adults touch 18-23 km/h. Values are estimated near zero and are flat for university/zonal women. This metric will barely separate tennis players.

matchAccelPerMin.note: Adolescent boys: high accelerations 0.6/min. Elite U16 boys: 56-58 accelerations of at least 2 m/s² per match. Neither study used the 3 m/s² threshold, so the ladder is estimated around these values.

sources: Kovalchik & Reid (2017) Comparing Matchplay Characteristics and Physical Demands of Junior and Professional Tennis Athletes in the Era of Big Data, J Sports Sci Med 16:489-497
card_firstInPct.note: Elite maps to international. At the 2017 Australian Open: pro men 63.7%, junior boys 59.3%; pro women 57.1%, junior girls 55.0%. At the 2023 Roland Garros: men ~61%. Levels are interpolated evenly from the approved 55 to 62. The women's elite value of 62 is above the observed pro average of ~57, but was kept as approved.

card_firstWonPct.note: Elite maps to international: pro men 72.1% and pro women 64.2% at the 2017 AO match the approved Elite targets almost exactly. Junior boys 66.7% sits at state level; junior girls 64.1% is already at the pro women's value. Even interpolation from the approved University values.

card_secondWonPct.note: Pro men 50.4% / junior boys 47.3%, and pro women 45.6% / junior girls 44.3% (2017 AO), so Elite maps to international. At the 2023 Grand Slams, male winners won 54-55% and losers 44%. Even interpolation.

card_acePct.note: Aces per service point at the 2017 AO: pro men 8.0%, junior boys 3.6%, pro women 3.8%, junior girls 2.8%. Elite maps to international. Evidence suggests the men's approved University target of 5 is high, since elite junior boys averaged only 3.6%. It was kept as approved.

card_dfPct.note: The 2017 AO double faults per service point (pro men 3.8%, junior boys 4.9%, pro women 5.0%, junior girls 5.4%) were converted per second serve using first-serve-in %. That gives pro men ~10.5%, junior boys ~12.0%, pro women ~11.7%, junior girls ~12.0%. Elite maps to international. Lower is better, and the ladder falls evenly from the approved 15.

card_wue.note: At the 2023 Roland Garros and US Open, male match winners averaged ~1.1-1.2 and losers ~0.76-0.81 (overall ~0.9-1.0). Tennis Abstract: 1.2 for men and 0.85 for women each go with ~70% match wins. The approved Elite (1.3 / 0.85) is a strong tour value, so it maps to international. Even interpolation.

card_netWonPct.note: 2023 Roland Garros and US Open men: winners 70.2%, losers 61.3-63.6%, averaging about 66-67% (the approved Elite). This maps to international. No women's or sub-elite net data was found, so the women's ladder and lower levels are interpolated evenly from the approved targets.

card_bpConvPct.note: Set to null under rule 4: the level average falls as opposition gets stronger, because better servers are harder to break. At the 2017 AO: junior boys 42.9% vs pro men 37.5%, junior girls 44.4% vs pro women 42.9%. Approved targets (M 35→40, W 40→45) are not used as a ladder; university-level averages are likely above them.

card_bpSavedPct.note: The mirror of break-point conversion, which rises with level. At the 2017 AO: pro men ~62.5% saved vs junior boys ~57.1%; pro women ~57.1% vs junior girls ~55.6%. Elite maps to international (approved 60 / 54, slightly below the pros). Even interpolation.

card_returnWonPct.note: Set to null under rule 4. A level's average return-points-won equals 100 minus its serve-points-won, and serve dominance grows with level. From the 2017 AO serve stats: junior boys ~41% vs pro men ~36%, junior girls ~45% vs pro women ~44%. The approved targets (M 35→38, W 40→43) even sit below what a typical university returner would post.

card_effForehand.note: No published data uses this (+ minus -) / attempts coding. Elite maps to international to match the other card stats. Even interpolation from the approved University (0) to Elite (20).

card_effBackhand.note: No published data uses this coding. Elite maps to international, with even interpolation from the approved -5 to 15.

card_effDefence.note: No published data uses this coding. Elite maps to international, with even interpolation from the approved -10 to 10.

sources: Kalpana K, Cherian KS, Khanna GL (2022) Energy availability and RED-S risk assessment among Kho-Kho players in India, Sport Sciences for Health
sprint30m.note: Men national = published 4.51 s 30 m sprint (n=52 national male players, Kalpana 2022). University men estimated from intercollegiate 50 m 7.09 s (Singh & Dubey 2016); international extrapolated. Women estimated ~11% slower, consistent with 18-23 y club/university women's 50 m 8.34 s (Kapas & Paul 2022).

sources: Das S, Sekh N (2025) A Comparative Status on Selected Physiological and Motor Variables of Different Level Women Kho-Kho Players in West Bengal, IJFMR 7(3)
shuttleRun.note: Women state/national = published 4x10 m (block pick-up) 11.20 / 10.15 s (Das & Sekh 2025); university blends their district 12.38 s with club/university women 11.34 s (Kapas & Paul 2022). Men estimated ~8% faster; college men 11.44 s (Paudyal 2023, Nepal) is the slow bound. Protocols vary a lot between Indian studies.

standingBroadJump.note: College men 2.02 m (Paudyal 2023) sets the low end; national men estimated ~2.40 m from their 44-47 cm vertical jump (Kalpana 2022). Women: district 1.87 m published (Das & Sekh 2025); their state 2.12 / national 2.55 m were discounted as implausible (national women above national men, SD only 0.07-0.15 m), so women set ~17% below men.

sitAndReach.note: Women published district 27.7 / state 34.2 / national 38.9 cm (Das & Sekh 2025), mapped university/state/national. Men estimated ~6 cm lower (usual sex gap); male kho-kho studies use incompatible box zeros (e.g. 5.9 in university men, Pandey 2016), so not used directly.

sources: Tyagi S, Vanaik A, Kumar A (2018) Physical and anthropometric characteristics of national level male runners of kho-kho game, International Journal of Applied Research 4(5):490-492
heightCm.note: National men 168.9 cm (n=100, Tyagi 2018) and ~164-168 cm (n=52, Kalpana 2022) -> national 168; height barely separates levels in kho-kho so the male ladder is near-flat. Women: West Bengal district/state/national 158.5/162.6/165.7 cm (SD ~1 cm, implausibly tight) blended with 18-23 y club/university women 153.5 cm (Kapas & Paul 2022).

matchMetresPerMin.note: No kho-kho GPS/time-motion study found (searched Indian journals). Estimated for a defender's active bout on a 27x16 m court (near-continuous running broken by pole turns and dodges), kept inside the app's 60-140 anchors; women ~8% lower. Chasers sitting in the squares will read far lower, so compare like with like.

matchTopSpeedKmh.note: Estimated. Longest straight in kho-kho is ~20-24 m (post to post), so peaks sit well below football; a 4.5 s 30 m sprinter reaches ~25-27 km/h over that distance.

matchHsrPerMin.note: Estimated (>15 km/h). Short straights and constant direction changes limit time above 15 km/h; no kho-kho tracking data exists to calibrate.

matchSprintMetresPerMin.note: Estimated (>20 km/h). Only the active chaser's lane sprints and long dives cross 20 km/h, so values are small; treat as low-confidence.

matchAccelPerMin.note: Estimated (>3 m/s^2). Kho-kho is dominated by bursts: kho-and-go starts, pole turns and dodges, so acceleration counts are relatively high for the distance covered.

card_touchSuccess.note: Directorate targets kept (University 35, Elite 50 -> international), even interpolation. No published attempt counts exist; UKK only publishes successful outs. One set for mat and traditional.

card_chaserOuts.note: Elite 3 mapped to international. UKK scores every out at 2 pts; league-leading attackers (Indian internationals) scored 84-108 pts a season, ~3.5-5 outs/match, so a typical international at 3 is consistent. Between levels interpolated.

card_diveShare.note: Elite 60 mapped to international. UKK (mat) top attackers took 65-75% of outs by pole/sky dive (e.g. Ramji Kashyap S2: 58 of 84 pts from dives), so league leaders sit just above. Dives are likely rarer on mud grounds, but no data quantifies it, so one set is kept.

card_khoQuality.note: Directorate targets kept (University 25, Elite 40 -> international), even interpolation. No published kho-grading data found.

card_khoFoul.note: Lower is better. Directorate targets kept (University 10, Elite 5 -> international), even interpolation. No published foul-kho rates found.

card_defendTime.note: Elite 100 mapped to international. UKK S1 best defenders (India internationals) averaged ~101-106 s/match (e.g. 20:23 over 12 matches; 1:43/match), which matches Elite 100 closely. Between levels interpolated.

card_avgRun.note: Directorate targets kept (University 45, Elite 75 -> international), even interpolation. UKK does not publish runs per match, so per-run time could not be checked.

card_notOutPct.note: Directorate targets kept (University 10, Elite 20 -> international), even interpolation. No published survival-to-end-of-turn rates found.

card_defErrors.note: Lower is better. Directorate targets kept (University 0.5, Elite 0 -> international), even interpolation. No published error counts found.

card_dodgeEff.note: Directorate targets kept (University 0, Elite 30 -> international), even interpolation. No published dodge-outcome data found.
